pairs.b: archive:archive:need_blind_compaction_audit: Need-Blind by Construction: A Counterfactua
pairs.prior_text: archive:need_blind_compaction_audit: Need-Blind by Construction: A Counterfactual Audit of What Agent Context Compaction Drops, and Why Summary Fidelity Does Not Predict Task Success. The task-success loss that context compaction causes in long-horizon tool-use agents is concentrated in a small set of load-bearing history items (identifiable by counterfactual masking of the history), LLM summarizers retain load-bearing items at no higher rate than non-load-bearing ones (they are need-blind), and therefore load-bearing retention, not compression ratio or summary fidelity, predicts the success loss; a pinning rule derived from counterfactual need labels on disjoint task types recovers most of the loss at matched tokens, whereas same-size recency or salience pinning does not. Every compaction scheme for long-horizon agents (LLM summarization, deterministic eviction, indexed archives, parallel blocks, learned compaction) is evaluated by end-task success, so what a locally plausible summary discards, and how often the discarded item is one a later step needs, is unmeasured beyond the single governance-constraint case. We propose a counterfactual audit: for reference episodes solved with full context, we mask each pre-boundary history item individually at a fixed compaction boundary and measure, first by teacher-forced action divergence at every later step and then by paired stochastic continuations, whether removing that item changes the agent's later actions and success. Items whose removal lowers continuation success are load-bearing. We then apply six compaction families at the same boundary and measure each family's retention of load-bearing versus non-load-bearing items (entailment judge validated against human annotation), its generic fidelity (ROUGE, LLM-judge faithfulness, compression ratio) and its paired downstream success loss. The central claim is that LLM summarizers are need-blind: their retention rate for load-bearing items equals their retention rate for everything else, so their success loss is explained by load-bearing drop events and not by fidelity metrics. As a constructive test, we learn a type-level pinning rule from need labels on one split of ALFWorld task types and apply it on held-out types at matched total tokens, against random, recency, salience and task-statement-only pinning and against an oracle that pins the counterfactual load-bearing set. We run 8B, 27B-class dense and 120B MoE open-weight backbones on ALFWorld (primary) and WebShop, with paired designs, null replicates and pre-registered thresholds.
pairs.label: distinct
pairs.reason: B studies within-episode context compaction, asking which history items are load-bearing and whether summarizers retain them; A studies whether a rule-compiled cross-episode statistic from a trajectory bank beats retrieved trajectories. Different objects (episode history vs experience bank), different mechanisms (need-blind dropping vs aggregation retrieval cannot carry).

pairs.prior_text: archive:retrieved_set_disagreement_gate: Abstain When They Disagree: Harm from Organically Accumulated Agent Memory Lives in the Retrieved Set, Not the Item, and a Disagreement Gate Beats Item-Level Utility Filtering at Zero Clean-Setting Cost. When a bank is accumulated organically over a task stream with no planted conflicts, the items that break tasks are not individually low-utility; harm concentrates in retrievals where the top-k items disagree about the next action for the current state. A read-time gate that abstains from injection when a cheap action-consistency score over the retrieved set falls below a threshold, with no extra LLM call, removes at least 70 percent of the natural paired harm while keeping at least 80 percent of the gain on agreeing retrievals, whereas item-level utility filtering, validity or provenance and recency gating, spurious-cue calibration, learned abstention and reliance steering do not, because they act on item properties that do not predict which retrievals break tasks. Every proposed defence against harmful retrieved memory acts on items: utility scores, validity or provenance states, recency, spurious-cue calibration, a learned abstain decision, or a global reliance setting. We test the alternative that harm from an organically accumulated experience bank is a property of the retrieved set. Over three randomized ALFWorld task streams, a 27B agent accumulates raw and distilled items through a ReMe-style write path with no planted conflicts, and banks are frozen at three checkpoints so staleness arises naturally. On held-out tasks every retrieval is labelled post hoc from expert plans and bank timestamps at the item level (right, wrong, stale, conflicting) and at the set level (agree-right, agree-wrong, disagree), and per-retrieval harm is estimated with paired no-memory runs and Entry-Propagation-Recovery tallies. A likelihood-ratio test asks which label explains broken outcomes. Eight read-time controls are then run head to head on the same seeds and banks: a disagreement gate based on a cheap action-consistency score, MemRL-style utility filtering, validity and provenance or recency gating, CAMEL-style calibration, an RSCB-MC-style learned abstain policy, reliance-steering instructions, an LLM-judge conflict verifier, and an oracle gate, each scored on harm removed, gain retained, clean-setting cost on agree-right retrievals, and token cost. A by-product is the first task-execution partition of failures into wrong retrieval, arbitration failure, and failure to apply a correctly retrieved item.

pairs.b: archive:archive:decorative_retriever: When Is a Retriever Decorative? Retrieval-Set Over
pairs.prior_text:
archive:decorative_retriever: When Is a Retriever Decorative? Retrieval-Set Overlap Predicts Whether Procedural Agent Memory Must Be Retrieved or Can Be Frozen. Per-instance retrieval in procedural agent memory (ExpeL/ReasoningBank/Memp-style) is decorative in exactly the regimes the field evaluates in, and there is a cheap, pre-deployment statistic that says when. Concretely: (a) **the frozen-subset swap** — replacing top-k retrieval with the *same k items, fixed for every query, verbatim, no LLM rewriting* — costs <2 accuracy points in every cell whose measured top-k retrieval-set Jaccard overlap exceeds 0.5; (b) that same overlap statistic, computable from the retriever alone in seconds with zero agent rollouts, predicts the retrieval premium **out of sample** across ~20 cells spanning overlap 0.05–1.0, with all overlap<0.25 cells showing a premium ≥8 points; and (c) the sign of the injection-volume effect is the *same* function of overlap — more retrieved items hurt at high overlap and help at low overlap, which reinterprets ReasoningBank's own "retrieving more memories hurts" ablation (49.7%@k=1 → 44.4%@k=4) as a redundancy artifact of a low-diversity retrieval set rather than a general "quality over quantity" law. One measured quantity, two phenomena, no agent runs required to predict either. Procedural agent memory is built as a retrieval system — distil training episodes into a bank, retrieve top-k per instance, inject — and every evaluation we can find compares it against *no memory*. Nobody re-runs the agent with the retriever replaced by a fixed subset of its own bank.

We do, and we do it across a designed sweep of retrieval-set diversity. The centerpiece is the **frozen-subset swap**: hold the agent, tools, decoding, bank, item count and injected tokens fixed, and replace per-instance top-k retrieval with the *k most frequently retrieved items on a dev split, verbatim, identical for every query*. No frontier model touches this arm, so a null cannot be attributed to a clever compiler. We run this swap in ~20 cells spanning measured top-k Jaccard overlap from ~0.05 to 1.0, moving overlap by four independent knobs — task-family breadth (single ALFWorld task type vs. all six vs. a mixed ALFWorld+multi-hop-QA bank), bank size (N=100→1000), retriever (dense vs. BM25 vs. MMR-diversified), and injection budget (k∈{1,3,7}) — plus a non-compilable near-duplicate bank as the low-overlap anchor.

Three claims, in order of how much of the paper they carry. **(i)** Wherever overlap > 0.5, the frozen-subset swap costs < 2 points (TOST equivalence at a 4-point margin; random-effects meta-estimate CI excluding 4). **(ii)** Overlap, computed from the retriever alone with zero agent rollouts, predicts the retrieval premium *out of sample* (leave-one-cell-out, permutation-tested against a grand-mean predictor), with a fitted crossing threshold — this is a deployable diagnostic, not a benchmark number. **(iii)** The sign of the injection-volume effect is the same function of overlap, which reinterprets ReasoningBank's published k-ablation (49.7%@k=1 → 44.4%@k=4, read as "quality over quantity") as a redundancy artifact, and makes an opposite-sign prediction to the interference account of Neural Procedural Memory (2606.29824) in an MMR-retriever cell we run.

We implement both ExpeL-style and ReasoningBank-style bank construction, token-match every static arm to the retrieval arm per instance, include an off-domain compiled control to rule out "any well-written static block of this length helps," and pre-register gates under which the study is reported as uninterpretable. ~23k evaluation episodes, three base models (8B/14B/32B), instance-paired McNemar and TOST, null replicates, stated MDE. No prompt optimizer is run; that arm was cut on purpose.
pairs.label: same_mechanism_new_measurement
pairs.reason: Both hold that per-instance retrieval is decorative unless the retrieved content must vary with the instance, and that a fixed/compiled substitute then matches it; but A causally manipulates that condition by editing the PDDL initial state (binding demand) and the bank's same-scene supply, and tests a compiled location table, where B only measures retrieval-set Jaccard overlap and a frozen-subset swap. The causal manipulation and the compiled-table recovery would change a reader's conclusion about why retrieval is decorative.

pairs.prior_text: archive:stall_triggered_injection: Retrieve When Stuck, Not When Starting: Injection Timing Sets the Sign of Experience Memory's Effect on Agent Traces, and a Two-Parameter Stall Trigger Matches a Learned Retrieval Policy. For a fixed bank, fixed query, fixed k and the very same retrieved items, revealing the items at the first detected stall (repeated, invalid or state-preserving action) instead of at the first decision point flips the paired effect on ALFWorld from harm-or-null to gain, because at a stall the agent has its own trajectory evidence to arbitrate against wrong items whereas at entry it must comply blind. A swept two-parameter static stall trigger (stall length n, injection cap M) lands inside the seed-noise band of MemCon-style and RSCB-MC-style learned when-to-retrieve policies at lower token cost, and transfers across backbones (8B, 27B, 120B) and to WebShop without relearning, whereas the learned policies must be relearned. Experience memories for LLM agents almost always inject retrieved items at episode start, and the recent alternative is a learned policy that decides when or whether to retrieve. Neither literature asks whether the time of injection alone changes the sign of memory's effect for the same items, and no learned policy has been compared with a tuned static trigger. We fix the bank, the query, k and the retrieved items, and vary only the reveal time: episode start, first detected stall, fixed late step, every step, reimplemented MemCon-style and RSCB-MC-style learned policies, and an oracle-timed upper bound, on ALFWorld and WebShop with three local backbones. Paired McNemar tests on identical task-seed pairs separate timing from content; a stall-triggered generic-reflection control and a stall-triggered random-item control separate memory content from a replanning nudge. Entry-Propagation-Recovery tallies against ALFWorld's expert plans test the mechanism: compliance rates should be similar across arms, but success conditional on compliance should be much higher at a stall than at entry. We then sweep the static trigger's two parameters on one backbone, freeze it, and swap backbones and environments, comparing against the learned policies frozen and relearned. The deliverable is a pre-registered answer to whether when-to-retrieve is a learning problem or a two-number heuristic, and whether the pilot's start-of-episode harm is a timing artefact.
pairs.label: distinct
pairs.reason: A varies the scope of instance bindings and the bank's supply of scope-matched items to determine the compiled substitute for retrieval; B varies only the reveal time of a fixed retrieved set and claims timing flips the sign of memory's effect. Different manipulated variable and mechanism.

A swept two-parameter static stall trigger (stall length n, injection cap M) lands inside the seed-noise band of MemCon-style and RSCB-MC-style learned when-to-retrieve policies at lower token cost, and transfers across backbones (8B, 27B, 120B) and to WebShop without relearning, whereas the learned policies must be relearned. Experience memories for LLM agents almost always inject retrieved items at episode start, and the recent alternative is a learned policy that decides when or whether to retrieve. Neither literature asks whether the time of injection alone changes the sign of memory's effect for the same items, and no learned policy has been compared with a tuned static trigger. We fix the bank, the query, k and the retrieved items, and vary only the reveal time: episode start, first detected stall, fixed late step, every step, reimplemented MemCon-style and RSCB-MC-style learned policies, and an oracle-timed upper bound, on ALFWorld and WebShop with three local backbones. Paired McNemar tests on identical task-seed pairs separate timing from content; a stall-triggered generic-reflection control and a stall-triggered random-item control separate memory content from a replanning nudge. Entry-Propagation-Recovery tallies against ALFWorld's expert plans test the mechanism: compliance rates should be similar across arms, but success conditional on compliance should be much higher at a stall than at entry. We then sweep the static trigger's two parameters on one backbone, freeze it, and swap backbones and environments, comparing against the learned policies frozen and relearned. The deliverable is a pre-registered answer to whether when-to-retrieve is a learning problem or a two-number heuristic, and whether the pilot's start-of-episode harm is a timing artefact.
pairs.label: distinct
pairs.reason: A is a cost claim: under prefix caching the ranking of static, whole-bank and retrieved prefixes is set by distinct-prefix count and decode-time context length, so matched-token budgets mis-rank routes. B is an accuracy/timing claim about when items are revealed. No shared mechanism.

pairs.b: archive:archive:opposite_sided_failure_under_shift: Stale in Context, Eroded in Weights:
pairs.prior_text: archive:opposite_sided_failure_under_shift: Stale in Context, Eroded in Weights: In-Context and Parametric Experience Fail on Opposite Sides of a Distribution Shift, and Only One Failure Is Predictable from the Bank. Over a task stream with a mid-stream conflicting shift that makes stored procedures wrong, an in-context experience store's post-shift dip is a read-path phenomenon whose size tracks the fraction of retrieved items that are pre-shift, that self-corrects once post-shift items dominate retrieval, and that costs pre-shift competence nothing; a parametric store built by continual LoRA on the same stream's successes shows no retrieval-fraction dependence, recovers as a function of update count, and erodes pre-shift competence monotonically with post-shift updates unless replay is paid. The two substrates fail on opposite sides of the shift, and the in-context failure is predictable from bank composition alone. The parametric and in-context substrates for agent experience are each said to have a stability-plasticity problem, but they have never been run on the same stream with the same shift, and their failures are described with the same word, forgetting, although they cannot be the same mechanism: a bank forgets nothing and a LoRA retrieves nothing. We build a 600-episode ALFWorld stream with three phases (original rules, a conflicting shift, revert) and two shift types: an action-grammar change that makes stored trajectories syntactically wrong, and a benign task-mix change where stale items are merely irrelevant. On one 7B backbone we run six substrates through the same stream: in-context banks with raw, utility-scored and recency-weighted retrieval; continual LoRA on the stream's successes with and without a costed replay budget; and a no-memory control. Every 50 episodes a frozen probe evaluates each substrate on held-out tasks under current-phase rules and under phase-1 rules, paired across substrates. For the in-context substrate we log, per probe, the fraction of retrieved items that are pre-shift and label each item right, stale-wrong or irrelevant; for the parametric substrate we log update count and replay tokens. The pre-registered predictions are that the in-context dip is explained by stale fraction and vanishes when it is zero, that its recovery time is predictable from bank composition, that parametric erosion of phase-1 competence grows with post-shift updates while the bank's does not, and that the benign shift produces neither. The preservation cost of each substrate at matched recovery is reported in tokens and GPU-seconds. The result is the first opposite-sided characterization of the two substrates on the same stream and a bank-composition predictor for in-context drag.
pairs.label: distinct
pairs.reason: Both use bank composition as a predictor, but A's claim is about near-miss confusability determining where whole-bank-in-context loses to top-k retrieval on a static bank, while B's is about in-context versus parametric stores failing on opposite sides of a mid-stream distribution shift, with staleness as the composition variable. Different manipulations, different comparison axes.

pairs.prior_text: archive:retrieved_set_disagreement_gate: Abstain When They Disagree: Harm from Organically Accumulated Agent Memory Lives in the Retrieved Set, Not the Item, and a Disagreement Gate Beats Item-Level Utility Filtering at Zero Clean-Setting Cost. When a bank is accumulated organically over a task stream with no planted conflicts, the items that break tasks are not individually low-utility; harm concentrates in retrievals where the top-k items disagree about the next action for the current state. A read-time gate that abstains from injection when a cheap action-consistency score over the retrieved set falls below a threshold, with no extra LLM call, removes at least 70 percent of the natural paired harm while keeping at least 80 percent of the gain on agreeing retrievals, whereas item-level utility filtering, validity or provenance and recency gating, spurious-cue calibration, learned abstention and reliance steering do not, because they act on item properties that do not predict which retrievals break tasks. Every proposed defence against harmful retrieved memory acts on items: utility scores, validity or provenance states, recency, spurious-cue calibration, a learned abstain decision, or a global reliance setting. We test the alternative that harm from an organically accumulated experience bank is a property of the retrieved set. Over three randomized ALFWorld task streams, a 27B agent accumulates raw and distilled items through a ReMe-style write path with no planted conflicts, and banks are frozen at three checkpoints so staleness arises naturally. On held-out tasks every retrieval is labelled post hoc from expert plans and bank timestamps at the item level (right, wrong, stale, conflicting) and at the set level (agree-right, agree-wrong, disagree), and per-retrieval harm is estimated with paired no-memory runs and Entry-Propagation-Recovery tallies. A likelihood-ratio test asks which label explains broken outcomes. Eight read-time controls are then run head to head on the same seeds and banks: a disagreement gate based on a cheap action-consistency score, MemRL-style utility filtering, validity and provenance or recency gating, CAMEL-style calibration, an RSCB-MC-style learned abstain policy, reliance-steering instructions, an LLM-judge conflict verifier, and an oracle gate, each scored on harm removed, gain retained, clean-setting cost on agree-right retrievals, and token cost. A by-product is the first task-execution partition of failures into wrong retrieval, arbitration failure, and failure to apply a correctly retrieved item.
pairs.label: distinct
pairs.reason: A claims many-shot whole-bank reading averages out per-item detour noise that top-k commits to, with detour rate and item count as the manipulated variables; B claims harm from organically accumulated banks is a set-level disagreement property and proposes a read-time abstention gate. Different noise source (detours vs conflicting actions), different intervention (read everything vs abstain), and neither claim entails the other.

pairs.b: archive:archive:decorative_retriever: When Is a Retriever Decorative? Retrieval-Set Over
pairs.prior_text:
archive:decorative_retriever: When Is a Retriever Decorative? Retrieval-Set Overlap Predicts Whether Procedural Agent Memory Must Be Retrieved or Can Be Frozen. Per-instance retrieval in procedural agent memory (ExpeL/ReasoningBank/Memp-style) is decorative in exactly the regimes the field evaluates in, and there is a cheap, pre-deployment statistic that says when. Concretely: (a) **the frozen-subset swap** — replacing top-k retrieval with the *same k items, fixed for every query, verbatim, no LLM rewriting* — costs <2 accuracy points in every cell whose measured top-k retrieval-set Jaccard overlap exceeds 0.5; (b) that same overlap statistic, computable from the retriever alone in seconds with zero agent rollouts, predicts the retrieval premium **out of sample** across ~20 cells spanning overlap 0.05–1.0, with all overlap<0.25 cells showing a premium ≥8 points; and (c) the sign of the injection-volume effect is the *same* function of overlap — more retrieved items hurt at high overlap and help at low overlap, which reinterprets ReasoningBank's own "retrieving more memories hurts" ablation (49.7%@k=1 → 44.4%@k=4) as a redundancy artifact of a low-diversity retrieval set rather than a general "quality over quantity" law. One measured quantity, two phenomena, no agent runs required to predict either. Procedural agent memory is built as a retrieval system — distil training episodes into a bank, retrieve top-k per instance, inject — and every evaluation we can find compares it against *no memory*. Nobody re-runs the agent with the retriever replaced by a fixed subset of its own bank.

We do, and we do it across a designed sweep of retrieval-set diversity. The centerpiece is the **frozen-subset swap**: hold the agent, tools, decoding, bank, item count and injected tokens fixed, and replace per-instance top-k retrieval with the *k most frequently retrieved items on a dev split, verbatim, identical for every query*. No frontier model touches this arm, so a null cannot be attributed to a clever compiler. We run this swap in ~20 cells spanning measured top-k Jaccard overlap from ~0.05 to 1.0, moving overlap by four independent knobs — task-family breadth (single ALFWorld task type vs. all six vs. a mixed ALFWorld+multi-hop-QA bank), bank size (N=100→1000), retriever (dense vs. BM25 vs. MMR-diversified), and injection budget (k∈{1,3,7}) — plus a non-compilable near-duplicate bank as the low-overlap anchor.

Three claims, in order of how much of the paper they carry. **(i)** Wherever overlap > 0.5, the frozen-subset swap costs < 2 points (TOST equivalence at a 4-point margin; random-effects meta-estimate CI excluding 4). **(ii)** Overlap, computed from the retriever alone with zero agent rollouts, predicts the retrieval premium *out of sample* (leave-one-cell-out, permutation-tested against a grand-mean predictor), with a fitted crossing threshold — this is a deployable diagnostic, not a benchmark number. **(iii)** The sign of the injection-volume effect is the same function of overlap, which reinterprets ReasoningBank's published k-ablation (49.7%@k=1 → 44.4%@k=4, read as "quality over quantity") as a redundancy artifact, and makes an opposite-sign prediction to the interference account of Neural Procedural Memory (2606.29824) in an MMR-retriever cell we run.

We implement both ExpeL-style and ReasoningBank-style bank construction, token-match every static arm to the retrieval arm per instance, include an off-domain compiled control to rule out "any well-written static block of this length helps," and pre-register gates under which the study is reported as uninterpretable. ~23k evaluation episodes, three base models (8B/14B/32B), instance-paired McNemar and TOST, null replicates, stated MDE. No prompt optimizer is run; that arm was cut on purpose.
pairs.label: distinct
pairs.reason: A bounds the value of when-to-retrieve policies by the mass of episodes where retrieval fails but the static prompt succeeds, and tests stall-triggered and failure-keyed retrieval; B is about whether the per-query selection itself can be frozen, with timing held at episode start throughout. Different decision variable (when vs which) and different mechanism.

pairs.b: archive:archive:instruction_conditioned_complementarity: What Does the Prompt Already Sa
pairs.prior_text: archive:instruction_conditioned_complementarity: What Does the Prompt Already Say? Instruction-Conditioned Complementarity Decides When Retrieved Experience Helps, Hurts, or Just Costs Tokens. The marginal value of an injected memory item is relational: it is determined by the item's content relative to what the agent's *instruction* already states, not by the item's similarity to the query nor by its similarity to other retrieved items. Labeling each unit of guidance in a retrieved item against the instruction as REDUNDANT (already asserted), NOVEL (instruction silent) or CONFLICTING (instruction asserts something incompatible) yields a three-way decomposition that predicts per-instance outcomes: fixes track novel units, breaks track conflicting units, redundant units are pure token cost. Consequences we test: (a) the *same* memory bank flips from helpful to inert when the instruction is optimized, because its units become redundant; (b) surgically deleting only the redundant units preserves accuracy at ~half the injected tokens while a token-matched random deletion does not; (c) deleting novel units destroys the fixes; (d) a retrieval rule that scores candidates by instruction-conditional novel-unit yield per token beats similarity top-k and item-diversity MMR at matched budget. Agentic memory retrieves past experience by similarity to the query and injects it alongside a task instruction that a prompt optimizer is separately rewriting. Both texts carry guidance; nothing in either pipeline checks whether they carry the *same* guidance. We propose that an item's marginal value is relational — it depends on what the instruction already says — and that this single variable explains the fix/break/token-cost structure of memory injection that recent empirical work documents but does not predict. We decompose the instruction and each retrieved item into atomic guidance units and label every item unit against the instruction as redundant, novel, or conflicting, using an off-the-shelf NLI model as the primary instrument (LLM and human labels used for validation only). We test three things on one environment with one primary model. First, relationality: holding the bank, retriever and retrievals fixed, we run under a short hand-written instruction and under an optimizer-produced long instruction, and predict that the same items flip from mostly novel to substantially redundant and that memory's paired gain collapses accordingly. Second, causality: unit-level surgery at matched token budget — delete only the redundant units, delete a token-matched random subset, delete the novel units, or delete a subset chosen against a *decoy* instruction — so the taxonomy can be falsified without touching the retriever. Third, exploitation: a complementarity retrieval rule scoring candidates by instruction-conditional novel-unit yield per token, against similarity top-k, MMR item-diversity, and a cheap embedding-overlap proxy at matched injected-token budgets. All comparisons are instance-paired with McNemar tests, null replicates, and a stated 5-point minimum detectable effect at n=500. The whole program is ~27k agent episodes on one 4×A100 node and under $100 of API.
pairs.label: distinct
pairs.reason: Both deny that query similarity predicts an item's value, but A's claim is that success is a step function of type match so the retriever reduces to a type classifier plus a similarity-scaled compliance hazard, tested by rank and leave-out ladders; B's is that value is relational to what the instruction already asserts, tested by redundant/novel/conflicting unit surgery. Different explanatory variable and different interventions.
